conceptTag: Interview a customer without leading them
readerTitle: How to hear the truth from a customer who wants to be nice
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (B2B 사무실 청소 회사 대표가 대기업 안 총무·시설팀 책임자를 인터뷰) + 실제 연구 (Loftus & Palmer, 1974 유도 질문 연구)
insight: 고객 인터뷰의 목적은 내 아이디어에 대한 의견을 듣는 것이 아니라, 고객이 실제로 겪은 일과 이미 한 행동을 듣는 것이다. 아이디어는 맨 마지막에 꺼내고, 칭찬이 아니라 작은 약속으로 확인한다.
misconception: 고객에게 '이런 서비스가 있으면 쓰시겠어요?'라고 직접 물어보면 수요를 확인할 수 있다. 고객이 '꼭 쓸게요'라고 하면 검증된 것이다.

sources.text: Loftus, E. F., & Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction: An example of the interaction between language and memory. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13(5), 585–589.
인터뷰 원칙 배경 참고: Fitzpatrick, R. (2013). The Mom Test. (카드 본문에는 책 이름을 쓰지 않고 원리만 다룸)
청소 회사, 보험사 총무팀, 인물과 대화는 모두 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Loftus & Palmer(1974) 실험 1: 'smashed'로 물은 집단의 평균 속도 추정이 약 40.5mph, 'hit'은 약 34.0mph로 보고됨. 카드에는 구체 수치 없이 '더 높은 속도를 추정했다'로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문으로 동사와 방향을 다시 확인하세요.
시뮬레이션의 모든 인물(Dana, Sam), 회사 규모(300명), 빈도(주 2회)는 가상입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 모든 시나리오 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.
테이크어웨이에서 각 결정을 유닛 개념(CUS-01-06, CUS-01-04, CUS-01-02, CUS-01-05)에 연결했습니다. 형제 레슨의 정의와 표현이 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Thirty minutes with a client who wants to be nice
body: Dana runs an office cleaning company. Her crews clean 30 offices every night. She has an idea: a daytime cleaner who keeps kitchens and meeting rooms tidy during work hours.

Before hiring anyone, she books 30 minutes with Sam. He runs the workplace team at a 300-person insurance firm, one of her biggest clients. He likes Dana. That's the problem. Four questions decide whether she hears the truth.

image.label: Two people talking over coffee in an office kitchen with a sink full of mugs
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 탕비실에서 청소 회사 대표(여성)와 고객사 총무 담당자(남성)가 커피를 들고 마주 앉아 대화. 뒤쪽 싱크대에 머그컵이 가득 쌓여 있음. 따뜻하고 친근한 분위기. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your opening question.
body: Sam is friendly and short on time. How does Dana open?

options.text: "Would you pay for a daytime cleaner?"
options.feedback: Sam will likely say "maybe" to be polite. Dana gets a guess about the future, framed around her idea, before she knows if there's a problem.

options.text: "Tell me about the last time something went wrong in the office between our visits."
options.feedback: Dana gets a real event with details. Sam talks about his week, not her idea.

options.text: "How do you feel about our cleaning overall?"
options.feedback: Safe and warm, but it invites a compliment. A happy client rarely criticizes you to your face.

cards.title: "It's mostly fine."
body: Say you chose B. Sam says: "Honestly, it's mostly fine. The kitchen gets a bit messy by afternoon."

options.text: "So a daytime kitchen cleaner would help, right?"
options.feedback: This hands Sam the answer. Agreeing is easier than explaining, so Dana hears her own idea echoed back.

options.text: "When did that last happen? What did you do?"
options.feedback: "A bit messy" is vague. A specific moment shows whether it's a small annoyance or a real headache.

options.text: "Got it. Let's move on to meeting rooms."
options.feedback: Dana covers more ground, but she'll never know how much the kitchen actually matters.

cards.title: The mugs before the meeting.
body: Say you chose B. Sam remembers last Thursday: a client visit, a sink full of mugs, and him washing them himself ten minutes before the meeting. He's tried a dish rota and a sign. Neither stuck.

options.text: Describe the daytime cleaner idea and ask what he thinks
options.feedback: Once Sam knows the idea, every answer bends toward it. And a client who likes Dana will praise it.

options.text: Ask how often it happens and what it costs him
options.feedback: Frequency and cost show how big the pain is. The rota and sign show he's already trying to fix it, so the need is real.

options.text: Ask how much he'd pay for a fix
options.feedback: Price matters, but asking now invites a made-up number. Learn the size of the problem first.

cards.title: "We'd definitely use that."
body: Say you chose B. About twice a week, Sam says, and it makes the firm look sloppy to clients. At the very end, Dana mentions her idea. Sam lights up: "That would be amazing. We'd definitely use it."

options.text: Count Sam as a yes and start hiring
options.feedback: Enthusiasm is free. A "definitely" at the end of a friendly chat is weak ground for a new hire.

options.text: Offer a paid two-week trial and ask who approves the budget
options.feedback: A small commitment tests whether the excitement is real. The budget question shows whether Sam can actually say yes.

options.text: Ask him to rate the idea from 1 to 10
options.feedback: Dana gets a number, but it's still an opinion. A 9 costs Sam nothing.

cards.title: Leading questions
body: A **leading question** hints at the answer you want. People tend to follow the hint, especially polite clients.

In a 1974 study, people watched film of a car crash. Those asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" gave higher speed estimates than those asked about cars that "hit". One word changed the answer.
The fix: ask about specific past events and what people did. Save your idea for the end, and test it with a commitment, not a compliment.

image.label: Two speech bubbles: a leading question versus an open question about the past
image.brief: 말풍선 두 개 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 빨간 테두리 "Would you use this?" 아래에 "Opinion about the future". 오른쪽 초록 테두리 "Tell me about the last time…" 아래에 "Facts about the past". 깔끔한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.softwareNote: Instead of "Would you use a reporting dashboard?", ask a user to share their screen and show how they built last month's report. Their spreadsheet workaround tells you more than any answer.

cards.title: Good interviews find problems. They don't prove demand.
body: Ten honest conversations can show a pain is real and common. They can't tell you how many customers will pay. That takes a trial, a pre-sale or real orders.
Memory is also imperfect. People forget details and tidy up their stories, so look for patterns across several interviews.
And the person feeling the pain may not hold the budget. Sam washes the mugs, but finance may sign. Talk to both.

cards.title: Ask about what happened, not what they'd do.
body: Each step in Dana's interview used an idea from this unit.
list: **Opening with a past event:** behavior beats opinions
**Digging into "a bit messy":** pains and gains, and how big the pain really is
**Asking about the rota and the sign:** the real job is looking professional in front of clients
**Offering a paid trial:** someone already hacking a fix may be an early adopter
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down the next question you plan to ask a customer. If it mentions your idea or the future, rewrite it to start with "Tell me about the last time…"
